blocks.text: **The problem.** Design a stack that supports `push(x)`, `pop()`, `top()`, and also `getMin()` and `getMax()` — the smallest and largest values **currently in the stack** — with **every operation in O(1) time**. `pop`, `top`, `getMin` and `getMax` are only called when the stack is non-empty. (LeetCode's **Min Stack** is this problem with only `getMin`; **Max Stack** adds more operations, but its core is the same idea.)

blocks.alt: A stack holding 5, 2, 8 and 1 from bottom to top. The minimum, 1, happens to be on top, but the maximum, 8, is buried one below the top. After popping 1, the minimum becomes 2, which is deeper still.

blocks.code:
push(5)  push(2)  push(8)  push(1)
getMin() -> 1    getMax() -> 8
pop()            // removes 1
getMin() -> 2    top() -> 8

blocks.text: The minimum and maximum can be **anywhere** in the stack, and they **change back** when items are popped. The trick is to remember what the min and max **were** at every height of the stack.
1. Brute force: scan the stack when asked
Keep a normal stack. When someone asks for the min or max, look at every item.
**push, pop, top O(1); getMin and getMax O(n).** Correct, but it breaks the O(1) requirement.
2. Optimal: every item remembers the min and max below it

When `x` is pushed, the min and max of the stack **from the bottom up to `x`** are easy to compute: compare `x` with the min and max stored in the item underneath. Store them **with** `x`. Popping an item then automatically restores the previous min and max — they were saved in the item below.

blocks.alt: Each stack entry stores a triple: value, min so far, max so far. Pushing 5 gives (5, 5, 5); 2 gives (2, 2, 5); 8 gives (8, 2, 8); 1 gives (1, 1, 8). The top entry's min and max are the answers.

elements.text: value | min so far | max so far
elements.originalText: value | min so far | max so far

blocks.text: **Every operation O(1); space O(n)** — but each item now takes three slots. Most of those saved mins and maxes are repeats of the one below.
3. Best solution: two helper stacks that only store records

Only store a min when it's a **new record**. Keep a helper stack `mins`: push `x` onto it only if `x` is **≤ the current minimum**. When popping, if the popped value **equals** the top of `mins`, pop `mins` too — that record has left the stack. A second helper `maxs` does the same for maximums with **≥**.

blocks.alt: Three stacks after pushing 5, 2, 8, 1. items holds 5, 2, 8, 1. mins holds only the records 5, 2, 1. maxs holds only the records 5, 8. The tops of mins and maxs are the current minimum and maximum.

elements.text: push x onto mins only if x <= min
elements.originalText: push x onto mins only if x <= min

elements.text: push x onto maxs only if x >= max
elements.originalText: push x onto maxs only if x >= max

elements.text: pop: if x equals a helper's top,
elements.originalText: pop: if x equals a helper's top,

blocks.text: Why **≤** and not **<**? Push 1 twice, then pop once. The minimum is still 1 — so the second 1 must have its own entry on `mins`; otherwise the first pop would remove the only record of 1 and `getMin` would wrongly jump to an older value.

blocks.caption: Try the repeated minimum example to see why ties are pushed onto mins.

blocks.text: **Every operation O(1); space O(n) in the worst case** (a strictly decreasing sequence makes every push a new minimum). In typical data, records are rare, so the helper stacks stay far shorter than `items`.

**Follow-up:** for Min Stack alone there is a well-known trick that needs **no helper stack**: when a new minimum arrives, store `2·x − oldMin` instead of `x`, and decode it on pop. It saves memory but can overflow 32-bit integers and only tracks one extreme, so the helper stacks are the safer interview answer.

rows.approach: Brute force: scan the stack when asked
rows.timeWhy: `getMin` and `getMax` **scan every item**; push, pop and top are O(1).

rows.approach: Optimal: every item remembers the min and max below it
rows.timeWhy: Each answer is **stored with the top item**, ready to read.

rows.approach: Best: two helper stacks that only store records
rows.timeWhy: Helpers change only when a **new record** is pushed or popped.
rows.spaceWhy: O(n) at worst, but usually far fewer records than items.

items: **Repeated minimum or maximum** — push 1, 1, pop: min must still be 1.
**Pop the current min** — the previous record must come back.
**A single item** — it is both the min and the max.
**Negative numbers** — no special cases; the brute force must start from ±infinity, not 0.
